lines.text: It's two a.m. at a hackathon. Kabir's chatbot finally works, and then his free API credits run out.
He doesn't need more credits. He needs a model that runs on his own laptop.
That's what Ollama does. It's a small server: it downloads open model weights, like Llama or Qwen, and loads them into memory.
Then it serves an API on localhost, right on his machine.
One command pulls a model. One more, and he's chatting in the terminal.
And here's the trick. Ollama speaks the same format as the OpenAI API.
So Kabir changes the base URL and the model name, and the rest of his code stays exactly the same.
Build and debug on the free local model, then flip one setting to a hosted model for the demo.
The catch is memory. Every weight must fit in RAM, so local models are quantised: about four bits per weight instead of sixteen.
On an eight gigabyte laptop, a three billion parameter model fits. Bigger models need more RAM.
What do you get? No bill, no internet, and nothing you type leaves the laptop.
What do you give up? It's smaller and slower than a hosted model, so test both on your own questions.
Remember it like this: same SDK, different base URL.
Next lesson: prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning?
